title: Fur
description: Soft, thick, hairy coat of a mammal
grok_lead: ![Down_Awn_and_guard_hairs_of_cat_2012_11_13_9203r.JPG][float-right] Fur is a thick, soft growth of specialized hairs covering the skin of most mammals, distinguishing them from other vertebrates and serving essential biological functions such as thermoregulation, protection from environmental elements, sensory perception, and camouflage. The mammalian coat typically comprises two primary layers: long, coarse, oily guard hairs that repel water and shield the undercoat, and a denser layer of short, fine underfur (including down and awn hairs) that traps air for insulation, enabling endothermic mammals to maintain body heat in diverse climates. Humans have harvested fur from animals for clothing and shelter since the Paleolithic era, approximately 180,000 years ago, valuing its natural waterproofing, durability, and thermal properties as critical for survival in cold environments long before synthetic alternatives existed. Archaeological evidence from Stone Age sites confirms fur's role in early garments, tools, and trade, evolving into a marker of status in ancient civilizations while remaining a practical material due to its renewable sourcing from hunted or trapped animals. In contemporary contexts, fur production encompasses wild trapping, which can support population control of overabundant species, and ranching, which has drawn scrutiny for potential welfare issues in confined breeding but contrasts with the environmental persistence of petroleum-derived faux furs; empirical assessments highlight fur's biodegradability and lower long-term ecological footprint when managed sustainably, countering narratives amplified by activist-driven sources often prioritizing emotive appeals over data on harvest efficiencies or comparative lifecycle impacts.
